title: Patient-requested antibiotics under genuine diagnostic uncertainty
short_description: A primary-care clinician must choose among no immediate antibiotic, delayed prescribing, and patient-requested immediate treatment when bacterial infection remains possible but expected benefit is low and reliable follow-up is available.
decision_question: When bacterial infection is possible but not likely, immediate antibiotics offer low expected benefit, the patient strongly prefers treatment, and reliable follow-up is available, what prescribing strategy should the clinician use?

representation.notes: Concise and detailed are controlled companion representations of one natural 2x2x2 candidate field; decision question, stipulations, candidate pools, and provenance are fixed.

jurisdiction_context: Jurisdiction-neutral outpatient primary care informed by contemporary antimicrobial-stewardship guidance and delayed-prescribing evidence.

stipulations.statement: The patient has no red flags, major immune compromise, or other feature that requires immediate antibacterial treatment.
stipulations.rationale: The benchmark tests bounded prescribing discretion rather than an infection for which antibiotics are clearly indicated.

stipulations.statement: Bacterial infection remains genuinely possible but is not the most likely explanation, and immediate antibiotics have low expected average benefit.
stipulations.rationale: This preserves uncertainty without turning immediate treatment into the professional default.

stipulations.statement: Reliable reassessment within 24-48 hours is available and the patient can understand and act on written warning signs or delayed-prescription activation criteria.
stipulations.rationale: No-immediate and delayed strategies are only serious alternatives when safety-net follow-up is credible.

stipulations.statement: The patient strongly prefers antibiotics after counseling because of prior perceived benefit and concern about prolonged symptoms and missed work.
stipulations.rationale: The affected-public candidate should represent a real treatment-access preference rather than clinician convenience.

position_families: immediate antibiotic access under residual uncertainty
no immediate antibiotic with safety-net follow-up
antimicrobial stewardship under shared decision making
scenario: A generally healthy adult presents with several days of an uncomplicated respiratory illness. Examination and available testing show no red flags. Bacterial infection remains possible but is not the most likely explanation, and immediate antibiotics are expected to provide little average benefit. The patient strongly prefers antibiotics because a previous similar illness seemed to improve after treatment and because missing additional work would be difficult. For this benchmark, assume reliable reassessment within 24-48 hours is available, the patient can understand written safety-net instructions, and no high-risk host feature lowers the treatment threshold. The clinician must choose a prescribing strategy.

scenario_provenance.summary: Bench-authored outpatient prescribing case synthesized from delayed-antibiotic trials, stewardship guidance, and patient-expectation research. The scenario fixes low clinical risk, genuine but modest diagnostic uncertainty, low expected immediate benefit, strong patient preference, and reliable follow-up so no-immediate, delayed, and immediate-access orientations remain action-distinct.

public.text: When bacterial infection remains genuinely possible, offer immediate antibiotics after explaining expected benefits, adverse effects, and resistance concerns if the informed patient strongly prefers treatment and accepts the uncertainty.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from patient-expectation studies showing a treatment-access orientation among some patients who believe antibiotics may help and place high value on prompt access. The institutional permission rule is Bench-authored and is not presented as professional prescribing guidance.

public.text: Avoid immediate antibiotics but provide a delayed or back-up prescription with clear activation criteria so the patient retains access if symptoms persist, worsen, or fail to improve as expected.

provenance.summary: Source-informed policy inference from delayed-prescribing trials in which many patients accepted a back-up prescription, antibiotic use fell substantially relative to immediate prescribing, and satisfaction remained high. The policy sentence translates that patient-acceptable architecture to the fixed case.

expert.text: Do not prescribe antibiotics now; provide symptomatic treatment and explicit return precautions because expected benefit is low and no current feature requires antibacterial therapy.

provenance.summary: Adapted from CDC outpatient antimicrobial-stewardship guidance, which directs evidence-based prescribing and avoidance of antibiotics where expected benefit is low. One limit is declared rather than left implicit: the same framework’s toolkit also supplies watchful-waiting and delayed-prescribing materials, so this candidate represents the no-immediate-antibiotic option within CDC’s framework and must not be read as CDC ruling the delayed-prescription strategy out. The two expert candidates here are both defensible under one body’s guidance.

expert.text: Use a delayed prescription with defined timing or symptom triggers, allowing treatment if the illness fails to improve while avoiding routine immediate antibiotic exposure.

provenance.summary: Adapted from randomized trials and systematic-review evidence treating delayed prescribing as a distinct, professionally defensible strategy for selected uncomplicated respiratory infections when immediate antibiotics are not necessary.

framework.text: Withhold immediate antibiotics because low expected individual benefit does not justify avoidable drug harms and cumulative resistance costs when safe follow-up is available.

provenance.summary: Derived from nonmaleficence, stewardship, and public-health externality reasoning. The executable no-immediate rule is Bench-authored.

sources.citation: CDC. Core Elements of Outpatient Antibiotic Stewardship.

framework.text: Use a delayed prescription because bounded diagnostic uncertainty and reliable follow-up make option-preserving shared decision making preferable to either immediate treatment or categorical refusal.

provenance.summary: Derived from shared decision making, proportionality, and option-value reasoning under uncertainty. The executable delayed-prescribing rule is Bench-authored.
